"Ask the sons of al-Asghar, if you come to them,
what the news of your father Abu Wasi' was.
May God not widen his grave,
but may God narrow it on the one who cut off [the ties of kinship].
The Messenger of God shot from among them,
apart from Quraysh, a shot of the one who strikes.
He deserved the prayer from him because of what
was made clear to the viewer and the listener.
So God set upon him His dog,
which walks with the gait of the deceiver,
until it reached him in the middle of his companions,
while sleep had marked them.
It seized the head by its crown,
and the throat from it was a hollow of the hungry one.
Then it rose after, with its teeth,
rolled in the dust, in the middle of thick blood.
This was a lesson for you,
for the lord who is followed and the follower.
Whoever returns this year to his family,
the lion's prey will not be the one who returns."
[[Dala'il al-Nubuwwah: 220, with variation; also in Majma' al-Bayan: 9/287.]]

﴿Your companion has neither gone astray nor erred﴾ [[Qur'an 53:2.]]. This is the answer to the oath.

﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [[Qur'an 53:3.]]. That is, "bi-al-hawa" (by desire); "'an" and "bi" are interchanged, so one takes the place of the other.

﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ [[Qur'an 53:4.]], that is, what he says concerning the religion is only a revelation revealed to him.

﴿Taught to him by one mighty in power﴾ [[Qur'an 53:5.]]. This is Jibril (Gabriel).

﴿Possessor of strength﴾ [[Qur'an 53:6.]]: power and might. A man "mirr" means strong. The poet said:

"You see the thin man and you despise him,
while in his garments there is a sturdy man."
[[Al-Sihah: 2/815.]]

Its origin is from "amarertu al-habl," when I twisted the rope tightly. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Charity is not lawful for the rich or for one who has sound strength (dhu mirrah sawiyy)." [116] [[Kanz al-'Ummal: 6/453, no. 16501.]]

Al-Kalbi said: Among his might was that he uprooted the cities of the people of Lot from the black water, carried them on his wing, raised them to the sky, and then overturned them. Among his might also was that he saw Iblis speaking with Isa on one of the mountains of the holy land, and he struck him with his wing, flinging him to the farthest mountain in India. Among his might also was his cry to Thamud, so they were in the morning lying prostrate and dead. Among his might also was his descent from heaven to the prophets and his ascent back to it more swiftly than a glance.

Qutrub said: The Arabs say of anyone of firm judgment, "hasif al-'aql" (sound of intellect). "Dhu mirrah" is also used in the words of the poet:

"Before meeting you, I was one of strength;
with me is his balance for every disputant."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 13/447.]]

It was from the soundness of his judgment and the firmness of his intellect that God the Exalted entrusted him with conveying His revelation to all His messengers.

Ibn Abbas said: ﴿Possessor of strength﴾, that is, one of fine appearance. Qatadah said: one of tall, fine form.

﴿Then he stood poised﴾ [[Qur'an 53:6.]]: this refers to Jibril. ﴿And he﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). In most Arabic speech, when they wish to coordinate in such a place, they make the pronoun of the thing coordinated with explicit, saying "istawa huwa wa-fulan" (he and so-and-so stood poised), not "istawa wa-fulan." Al-Farra' recited:

"Do you not see that the sturdy tree stands straight,
while the castor-oil plant, which is broken, does not stand?"
[[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 27/58.]]

The meaning: "He" is not equal to the castor-oil plant.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿When we are dust and our fathers﴾ [[Qur'an 56:47 / 23:82, as cited in the source.]], where "our fathers" is coordinated with the implicit pronoun in "kunna" without making "nahnu" explicit. The meaning of the verse: Jibril and Muhammad stood poised on the night of the Ascension ﴿at the highest horizon﴾ [[Qur'an 53:7.]], which is the farthest part of the world at the place of sunrise in the sky. It is also said: they stood poised in strength and in ascent to the sky. It is also said: they stood poised in knowledge of the revelation. Some have said: the meaning of the verse is: Jibril stood poised, that is, rose and ascended in the sky after he had taught Muhammad. This is from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. It is also said: ﴿istawa﴾ means he stood in his form in which God created him. That is because he used to come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the form of human beings, as he came to the prophets. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked him to show him himself in his true form, and he showed him himself twice: once on earth and once in heaven. On earth it was at the highest horizon, for Muhammad (ﷺ) was at Hira', and Jibril appeared to him from the east, filling the horizon to the west. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) fell unconscious. Jibril descended in the form of a human being, embraced him, and began to wipe the dust from his face. [117] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/87.]]

The proof of this is His saying: ﴿And he saw him at the clear horizon﴾ [[Qur'an 81:23.]]. As for in heaven, it was at the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha), and none of the prophets saw him in that form except Muhammad the Chosen, may God's blessings be upon him.

﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ [[Qur'an 53:8.]]. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of this verse. Some said: its meaning is: Then Jibril drew near after his standing at the highest horizon of the earth, ﴿and descended﴾, descending to Muhammad (ﷺ) with the revelation, and he swooped down upon him. ﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ [[Qur'an 53:9.]], that is: "bal adna" (rather, nearer). This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Rabi'.

The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: There is advancing and delaying in the speech. Its estimated meaning is: "Then he descended and drew near," because descent is drawing near; but it is a beautiful expression, since "tadalli" (descent) indicates nearness and nearness indicates descent. He descended for nearness and drew near for descent. Others said: its meaning is: Then the Lord, glory be to Him, drew near to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿and descended﴾, so He came near to him until he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer. The root of "tadalli" is descending toward a thing until one comes near to it, so it was used in place of nearness. Labid said:

"I descended upon him, returning,
while on the earth were the depths of the shadows."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 15/144.]]

This is the meaning of the saying of Anas and the report of Abu Salamah from Ibn Abbas.

'Aqil ibn Muhammad informed me that Abu al-Faraj al-Baghdadi informed them, from Muhammad ibn Jarir, who said: al-Rabi' told us, saying: Ibn Wahb told us, from Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Shurayk ibn Abi Namir, who said: I heard Anas ibn Malik narrating to us about the night of the journey (laylat al-masra), that Jibril took the Messenger of God (ﷺ) up to the seventh heaven, then ascended with him to what none knows except God, Mighty and Majestic, until he reached the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary. The Almighty, Lord of Might, drew near and descended, ﴿so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾, ﴿then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [[Qur'an 53:10.]]. The nearness of God to the servant and the nearness of the servant to Him is in rank, station, and position, and in answering the supplication and granting the desire, not in place, distance, or movement. Like His saying: ﴿Indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [[Qur'an 2:186.]].

Some said: its meaning is: Then Jibril drew near to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer. This is the saying of Mujahid, and it is supported by what is reported in the hadith: "He is the nearest of the angels to God, glory be to Him, after Jibril." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/90.]] [118]

Al-Dahhak said: ﴿Then he drew near﴾, meaning Muhammad drew near to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿and descended﴾, so he bowed for prostration, ﴿so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾. It was also said: Muhammad drew near to the leg of the Throne and ﴿descended﴾, that is, he approached the veils and the canopies, not a movement from place to place, and he stood by God's permission as one who clings to a thing without his foot being fixed in a place. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl.

The meaning of His saying ﴿qaba qawsayn﴾ is "the measure of two Arab bows," according to Ibn Abbas and Ata'. "Qab," "qayb," "qad," and "qid" are expressions for the measure of a thing, and its counterpart in speech is "zir" and "zar."

He (ﷺ) said: "The space of the bow of one of you in Paradise is better than this world and all that is in it." [119] [[Fath al-Bari: 4/85.]]

Mujahid said: It means where the string is on the bow. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "Qab" is the middle part of the Arab bow where the leather strap is tied, which its holder grips, and every bow has one qab. So He informed that the nearness of Jibril to Muhammad (ﷺ) at the time of revelation is like the nearness of the space of two bows.

The people of the meanings said: This is an indication of the confirmation of love and nearness and the elevation of rank and station. Its origin is that in the pre-Islamic period, two allies and lovers, when they wished to establish friendship, covenant, and faithfulness, would go out with their two bows, the friendship between them, meaning that they were mutually supportive and protective, each protecting his companion.

It was also said: This is a simile for bringing one thing close to another, and it is used in the proverbs and poetry of the Arabs. Sufyan ibn Salamah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ata', and Ibn Ishaq al-Hamdani said: ﴿Qaba qawsayn﴾ means the measure of two cubits, and "qaws" is the cubit by which everything is measured, and this is the dialect of some people of the Hijaz. ﴿Or nearer﴾, that is, "bal adna" (rather, nearer).

Some said: He only said ﴿or nearer﴾ because He did not intend to set a limited boundary for that.

Abu al-Abbas ibn Ata' was asked about this verse and said: How can I describe to you a station from which Jibril, Mika'il, and Israfil were cut off, and in which there was none but Muhammad and his Lord? Al-Kisa'i said: ﴿Qaba qawsayn﴾ means one bow, as the poet said:

"And two deserts, one broad and one narrow, twice,
I crossed them by the direction, not by two directions."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 2/46.]]

He meant one desert.

Some of the people of the meanings said: The meaning of His saying ﴿fa-tadalla﴾ is "tadallul" (coquetry), from "dalal," as they say: "tazunnu" with the meaning of "tazunnun," and "amlaa" and "amlal" with the same meaning.

﴿Then He revealed﴾: that is, God the Exalted revealed to ﴿His servant﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ) what He revealed.

Al-Hasan, al-Rabi', and Ibn Zayd said: The meaning is: Jibril revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) what his Lord revealed to him. Sa'id said: He revealed to him ﴿Did He not find you an orphan﴾ [[Qur'an 93:6.]] up to His saying ﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾ [[Qur'an 94:4.]]. It was also said: He revealed to him that Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until he enters it, and forbidden to the nations until his community enters it.

Abu al-Hasan al-Thawri was asked about it and said: He revealed to him a secret, a secret from a secret, within a secret. Concerning this the poet says:

"Between the lovers is a secret that no speech reveals,
nor a pen that describes it to the creation.
A secret mixed with intimacy, facing it,
a light bewildered in a sea of perplexity."
[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 9/289.]]

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ [[Qur'an 53:11.]]. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far [al-Jahdari], and Qatadah recited "kadhdhaba" with a doubled dhal, meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not deny what it saw with his eye that night, but confirmed and verified it. The rest recited it with the light form, "kadhaba," meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not lie about what he saw, but confirmed it. The figurative meaning of the verse is: "The heart did not lie concerning what it saw," so the attribute is dropped, as in the poet's words:

"If you had been truthful in what you told me,
you would have escaped as Harith ibn Hisham escaped."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/93.]]

That is: "in that which you told me." Bandar ibn al-Hasan said: "Al-fu'ad" is the vessel of the heart; "the heart doubted concerning what it saw" means the origin, which is the heart.

They differed about who was seen. Some said: He saw Jibril, and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud. Others said: It is God, the Exalted. Then they differed about the meaning of the seeing. Some said: He placed his sight in his heart, so he saw Him in his heart and did not see Him with his eye. Others said: Rather, he saw Him with his eye.

Mention of those who said he saw Him with his eye:

Al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn informed me, saying: al-Fadl ibn al-Fadl told us, saying: Abu Ya'la Muhammad ibn Zuhayr al-Ablli told us, saying: Ibn Nuhwayh told us, saying: Salamah told us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq told us, saying: Ibn al-Taymi told us, from al-Mubarak ibn Fudalah, who said: al-Hasan used to swear by God, Mighty and Majestic, that Muhammad had seen his Lord.

'Aqil ibn Muhammad also informed me, saying: al-Mu'afa ibn Zakariyya told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jarir told us, saying: Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Mahran told us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from one who heard Ibn Abbas say: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾, he said: Muhammad saw his Lord.

With his chain from Ibn Humayd: Yahya ibn Wadih told us, saying: Isa ibn Ubayd told us, saying: I heard Ikrimah, and he was asked: Did Muhammad see his Lord? He said: Yes, he saw his Lord.

Also from Ibn Humayd: Hakkam told us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', concerning ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾: he said: He saw his Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Mention of those who said he did not see Him:

Abu Ubayd Allah al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Hafiz informed us, by my reading to him in my house, saying: Musa ibn Muhammad ibn Ali told us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Zuhayr told us, saying: Makki ibn Ibrahim told us, saying: Musa ibn Ubaydah told us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: One of the companions of the Messenger of God said: O Messenger of God, did you see your Lord? He said: "I saw Him twice, with my heart, and I did not see Him with my eye." [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 27/62; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 4/268, where the known wording is: "I did not see Him with my eye, and I saw Him with my heart twice."]] [120] Then he recited this verse: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾.

Similar was reported from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, from his father, and from Abu al-Aliyah, from Ibn Abbas.

Al-Hasan informed me, saying: Abu al-Qasim told us, from Ibn Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Hatim al-Tirmidhi, who said: My maternal grandfather Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Marzuq told us, saying: Affan ibn Muslim told us, saying: Hammam ibn Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq told us, who said: I said to Abu Dharr: If I had seen the Messenger of God (ﷺ), I would have asked him. He said: And what would you have asked him? I said: I would have asked him: Did he see his Lord, Mighty and Majestic? He said: I have indeed asked him, and he said: "I saw a light; how could I see Him?" [[Sharh Muslim by al-Nawawi: 3/12; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/93; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 3/5, with some variation in the wording of the hadith.]] [121]

Likewise, it is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about "The heart did not lie in what it saw," and he said: "I saw a light."
[[al-Musdar al-Sabiq, .]] [122], and Mujahid and Ikrimah narrated the like from Ibn 'Abbas.

There is a comprehensive hadith on this subject, which al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan informed me of, saying: Ibn Habash narrated to us, saying: 'Ali ibn Zanjawayh informed us, saying: Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn 'Uyaynah informed us, from Mujalid, from Sa'id, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith, who said: Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b met, and Ibn 'Abbas said: As for us, the Banu Hashim, we say that Muhammad saw his Lord twice. Ibn 'Abbas said: They love that intimate friendship (khullah) be for Ibrahim, speech for Musa, and vision for Muhammad. He said: Then Ka'b exclaimed "Allahu akbar" until the mountains echoed back to him, and then said:
"Indeed Allah, glory be to Him, divided His vision and His speech between Muhammad and Musa, peace be upon him. Musa spoke with Him, and Muhammad saw Him."
Mujalid said: al-Sha'bi said: Masruq informed me that he said to 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "O mother, did Muhammad (ﷺ) ever see his Lord, may He be exalted?" She said: "You have said a dreadful thing; my hair stood on end at it." I said: "Gently. Then I recited to her: ﴿Then he drew near and came down, and was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾." She said: "Gently! Where are you going with this? He only saw Jibril in his true form. Whoever tells you that Muhammad saw his Lord has lied, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾. Whoever tells you that he knows the five matters of the Unseen has lied, and Allah, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour﴾, and the verse. Whoever tells you that Muhammad concealed any part of the revelation has lied, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿O Messenger, deliver what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾, and the verse."

'Abd al-Razzaq said: I mentioned this hadith to 'Umar, and he said: "'Aishah is not more knowledgeable than Ibn 'Abbas in our view."

﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ That is: over what he saw.

'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Aishah, Masruq, al-Nakha'i, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Ya'qub read ﴿Afatamrunahu﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and without an alif, meaning "Will you then deny him," and Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading, saying:
"Because they did not dispute with him; rather, they denied him. The Arabs say: 'Maraytu al-rajul haqqahu' when you denied the man his right." The poet said:
"If you have forsaken a brother of truthfulness and honor, you have indeed denied a brother who never denied you."
That is, you denied him.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Talhah ibn Musarrif read ﴿Afatumrunahu﴾ with a damma on the ta' and without an alif, meaning "Will you cause him doubt and make him suspicious." The rest read ﴿Afatumarunahu﴾ with the alif and a damma on the ta', meaning "Will you then argue with him," and this is the choice of Abu Hatim.

And in a hadith: "Do not dispute about the Qur'an, for disputing over it is disbelief."
[123] [[Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/619, no. 2860.]]

Makkan. It contains one thousand four hundred and five letters, three hundred and sixty words, and sixty-two verses.

Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Qasim ibn Ahmad informed me, by my reading to him, saying: Abu Muhammad Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Ja'far told us, saying: Abu Amr al-Hiri and Umar ibn Abdullah al-Basri informed us, the two of them saying: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab told us, saying: Ahmad ibn Abdullah ibn Yunus told us, saying: Salam ibn Sulaym told us, saying: Harun ibn Kathir told us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from Abu Umamah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Najm will be given the reward of ten good deeds for each person who has believed in Muhammad and each person who has denied him." [114] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 9/284.]]

In the Name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the star when it sets﴾. Ibn Abbas, in the narration of al-Walibi and al-Awfi, and Mujahid, in the narration of Ibn Abi Najih, said: It means the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) when they fall and set. The Arabs call the Pleiades a "najm" (star), even though they are many in number.

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Darbandi said: They are seven stars, six of which are visible and one of which is hidden, by which people test their eyesight. From this is the saying of the Arabs when the star rises in the evening: "The shepherd sought a cloak." It is also reported from Mujahid: It means all the stars of the sky until they set. Its wording is singular but its meaning is plural, like the words of al-Ra'i:

"So she began to count the stars in her dim place,
swift in the hands of those who eat their dried curds."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 12/570.]]

A star (kawkab) is called a "najm" because of its rising (tulu'), and everything that rises is a "najm." It is said: "The star (najm) of the rain, the drought, and the wilderness has risen" when it rises.

Ikrimah reported from Ibn Abbas that it is the meteor (rajm) among the stars, meaning that which is hurled at the devils when they eavesdrop. Al-Dahhak said: It means the Qur'an when it was revealed in three verses, four verses, and a surah, and the period between its beginning and its end was twenty-three years. This is the report of al-A'mash from Mujahid and of Hayyan from al-Kalbi. The Arabs call dispersal "tanjim" and the one who disperses "munajjim," and from this comes "nujum al-din" (the stars of religion).

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Muhammad ibn Khalaf told us, saying: Ishaq ibn Muhammad told us, saying: My father told us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Isa told us, saying: Ali ibn Ali told us, saying: Abu Hamzah al-Thumali told me: ﴿By the star when it sets﴾. He said: It is said that they are the stars when they scatter on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Akhfash said: It is the plant (al-nabt). From this is His saying: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [[Qur'an 55:6.]]. "Hawiyyah" means its falling to the ground, because it has no stem.

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: It means Muhammad (ﷺ) when he descended from the sky on the night of the Ascension (al-mi'raj).

"Al-hawiy" means descending and falling. It is said: "Hawa yahwi hawiyyan," meaning "madha yamdi madiyyan" (he passed on). Zuhayr said:

"With them the goats' hooves wounded, while they fall
like the falling of a bucket whose rope has let it go."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 2/304.]]

Urwah ibn al-Zubayr reported from men of his household, who said: The daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was married to Utbah ibn Abi Lahab. He wanted to travel to Syria, and said: "Muhammad is cut off (abtar), so I will harm him through his daughter." He came to him and said: "O Muhammad, I disbelieve in ﴿the star when it sets, and in him who drew near and then came down﴾ [[Qur'an 53:1, 53:8.]]." Then he spat in his face, returned his daughter to him, and divorced her. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O God, set upon him one of Your dogs." [[Al-Sunan al-Kubra: 5/211.]] [115] He said: Abu Talib was present, and he was dismayed by it and said:

"How rich you were, nephew, without this call."

Utbah returned to his father and told him of this. Then they set out for Syria and camped at a place, and a monk from the monastery overlooked them and said: "This is a land of wild beasts." Abu Lahab said to his companions: "Help us tonight, O people of Quraysh, for I fear for my son because of Muhammad's prayer." They gathered their loads, spread a bed for Utbah on top of them, and slept around him. A lion came and began to sniff their faces, then coiled its tail, leapt, struck Utbah with its paw, and seized him, scratching him. He said: "It has killed me," and died on the spot. Hassan ibn Thabit said about this:

"Ask the sons of al-Asghar, if you come to them,
what the news of your father Abu Wasi' was.
May God not widen his grave,
but may God narrow it on the one who cut off [the ties of kinship].
The Messenger of God shot from among them,
apart from Quraysh, a shot of the one who strikes.
He deserved the prayer from him because of what
was made clear to the viewer and the listener.
So God set upon him His dog,
which walks with the gait of the deceiver,
until it reached him in the middle of his companions,
while sleep had marked them.
It seized the head by its crown,
and the throat from it was a hollow of the hungry one.
Then it rose after, with its teeth,
rolled in the dust, in the middle of thick blood.
This was a lesson for you,
for the lord who is followed and the follower.
Whoever returns this year to his family,
the lion's prey will not be the one who returns."
[[Dala'il al-Nubuwwah: 220, with variation; also in Majma' al-Bayan: 9/287.]]

﴿Your companion has neither gone astray nor erred﴾ [[Qur'an 53:2.]]. This is the answer to the oath.

﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [[Qur'an 53:3.]]. That is, "bi-al-hawa" (by desire); "'an" and "bi" are interchanged, so one takes the place of the other.

﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ [[Qur'an 53:4.]], that is, what he says concerning the religion is only a revelation revealed to him.

﴿Taught to him by one mighty in power﴾ [[Qur'an 53:5.]]. This is Jibril (Gabriel).

﴿Possessor of strength﴾ [[Qur'an 53:6.]]: power and might. A man "mirr" means strong. The poet said:

"You see the thin man and you despise him,
while in his garments there is a sturdy man."
[[Al-Sihah: 2/815.]]

Its origin is from "amarertu al-habl," when I twisted the rope tightly. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Charity is not lawful for the rich or for one who has sound strength (dhu mirrah sawiyy)." [116] [[Kanz al-'Ummal: 6/453, no. 16501.]]

Al-Kalbi said: Among his might was that he uprooted the cities of the people of Lot from the black water, carried them on his wing, raised them to the sky, and then overturned them. Among his might also was that he saw Iblis speaking with Isa on one of the mountains of the holy land, and he struck him with his wing, flinging him to the farthest mountain in India. Among his might also was his cry to Thamud, so they were in the morning lying prostrate and dead. Among his might also was his descent from heaven to the prophets and his ascent back to it more swiftly than a glance.

Qutrub said: The Arabs say of anyone of firm judgment, "hasif al-'aql" (sound of intellect). "Dhu mirrah" is also used in the words of the poet:

"Before meeting you, I was one of strength;
with me is his balance for every disputant."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 13/447.]]

It was from the soundness of his judgment and the firmness of his intellect that God the Exalted entrusted him with conveying His revelation to all His messengers.

Ibn Abbas said: ﴿Possessor of strength﴾, that is, one of fine appearance. Qatadah said: one of tall, fine form.

﴿Then he stood poised﴾ [[Qur'an 53:6.]]: this refers to Jibril. ﴿And he﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). In most Arabic speech, when they wish to coordinate in such a place, they make the pronoun of the thing coordinated with explicit, saying "istawa huwa wa-fulan" (he and so-and-so stood poised), not "istawa wa-fulan." Al-Farra' recited:

"Do you not see that the sturdy tree stands straight,
while the castor-oil plant, which is broken, does not stand?"
[[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 27/58.]]

The meaning: "He" is not equal to the castor-oil plant.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿When we are dust and our fathers﴾ [[Qur'an 56:47 / 23:82, as cited in the source.]], where "our fathers" is coordinated with the implicit pronoun in "kunna" without making "nahnu" explicit. The meaning of the verse: Jibril and Muhammad stood poised on the night of the Ascension ﴿at the highest horizon﴾ [[Qur'an 53:7.]], which is the farthest part of the world at the place of sunrise in the sky. It is also said: they stood poised in strength and in ascent to the sky. It is also said: they stood poised in knowledge of the revelation. Some have said: the meaning of the verse is: Jibril stood poised, that is, rose and ascended in the sky after he had taught Muhammad. This is from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. It is also said: ﴿istawa﴾ means he stood in his form in which God created him. That is because he used to come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the form of human beings, as he came to the prophets. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked him to show him himself in his true form, and he showed him himself twice: once on earth and once in heaven. On earth it was at the highest horizon, for Muhammad (ﷺ) was at Hira', and Jibril appeared to him from the east, filling the horizon to the west. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) fell unconscious. Jibril descended in the form of a human being, embraced him, and began to wipe the dust from his face. [117] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/87.]]

The proof of this is His saying: ﴿And he saw him at the clear horizon﴾ [[Qur'an 81:23.]]. As for in heaven, it was at the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha), and none of the prophets saw him in that form except Muhammad the Chosen, may God's blessings be upon him.

﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾ [[Qur'an 53:8.]]. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of this verse. Some said: its meaning is: Then Jibril drew near after his standing at the highest horizon of the earth, ﴿and descended﴾, descending to Muhammad (ﷺ) with the revelation, and he swooped down upon him. ﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ [[Qur'an 53:9.]], that is: "bal adna" (rather, nearer). This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Rabi'.

The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: There is advancing and delaying in the speech. Its estimated meaning is: "Then he descended and drew near," because descent is drawing near; but it is a beautiful expression, since "tadalli" (descent) indicates nearness and nearness indicates descent. He descended for nearness and drew near for descent. Others said: its meaning is: Then the Lord, glory be to Him, drew near to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿and descended﴾, so He came near to him until he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer. The root of "tadalli" is descending toward a thing until one comes near to it, so it was used in place of nearness. Labid said:

"I descended upon him, returning,
while on the earth were the depths of the shadows."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 15/144.]]

This is the meaning of the saying of Anas and the report of Abu Salamah from Ibn Abbas.

'Aqil ibn Muhammad informed me that Abu al-Faraj al-Baghdadi informed them, from Muhammad ibn Jarir, who said: al-Rabi' told us, saying: Ibn Wahb told us, from Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Shurayk ibn Abi Namir, who said: I heard Anas ibn Malik narrating to us about the night of the journey (laylat al-masra), that Jibril took the Messenger of God (ﷺ) up to the seventh heaven, then ascended with him to what none knows except God, Mighty and Majestic, until he reached the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary. The Almighty, Lord of Might, drew near and descended, ﴿so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾, ﴿then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [[Qur'an 53:10.]]. The nearness of God to the servant and the nearness of the servant to Him is in rank, station, and position, and in answering the supplication and granting the desire, not in place, distance, or movement. Like His saying: ﴿Indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [[Qur'an 2:186.]].

Some said: its meaning is: Then Jibril drew near to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer. This is the saying of Mujahid, and it is supported by what is reported in the hadith: "He is the nearest of the angels to God, glory be to Him, after Jibril." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/90.]] [118]

Al-Dahhak said: ﴿Then he drew near﴾, meaning Muhammad drew near to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿and descended﴾, so he bowed for prostration, ﴿so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾. It was also said: Muhammad drew near to the leg of the Throne and ﴿descended﴾, that is, he approached the veils and the canopies, not a movement from place to place, and he stood by God's permission as one who clings to a thing without his foot being fixed in a place. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl.

The meaning of His saying ﴿qaba qawsayn﴾ is "the measure of two Arab bows," according to Ibn Abbas and Ata'. "Qab," "qayb," "qad," and "qid" are expressions for the measure of a thing, and its counterpart in speech is "zir" and "zar."

He (ﷺ) said: "The space of the bow of one of you in Paradise is better than this world and all that is in it." [119] [[Fath al-Bari: 4/85.]]

Mujahid said: It means where the string is on the bow. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "Qab" is the middle part of the Arab bow where the leather strap is tied, which its holder grips, and every bow has one qab. So He informed that the nearness of Jibril to Muhammad (ﷺ) at the time of revelation is like the nearness of the space of two bows.

The people of the meanings said: This is an indication of the confirmation of love and nearness and the elevation of rank and station. Its origin is that in the pre-Islamic period, two allies and lovers, when they wished to establish friendship, covenant, and faithfulness, would go out with their two bows, the friendship between them, meaning that they were mutually supportive and protective, each protecting his companion.

It was also said: This is a simile for bringing one thing close to another, and it is used in the proverbs and poetry of the Arabs. Sufyan ibn Salamah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ata', and Ibn Ishaq al-Hamdani said: ﴿Qaba qawsayn﴾ means the measure of two cubits, and "qaws" is the cubit by which everything is measured, and this is the dialect of some people of the Hijaz. ﴿Or nearer﴾, that is, "bal adna" (rather, nearer).

Some said: He only said ﴿or nearer﴾ because He did not intend to set a limited boundary for that.

Abu al-Abbas ibn Ata' was asked about this verse and said: How can I describe to you a station from which Jibril, Mika'il, and Israfil were cut off, and in which there was none but Muhammad and his Lord? Al-Kisa'i said: ﴿Qaba qawsayn﴾ means one bow, as the poet said:

"And two deserts, one broad and one narrow, twice,
I crossed them by the direction, not by two directions."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 2/46.]]

He meant one desert.

Some of the people of the meanings said: The meaning of His saying ﴿fa-tadalla﴾ is "tadallul" (coquetry), from "dalal," as they say: "tazunnu" with the meaning of "tazunnun," and "amlaa" and "amlal" with the same meaning.

﴿Then He revealed﴾: that is, God the Exalted revealed to ﴿His servant﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ) what He revealed.

Al-Hasan, al-Rabi', and Ibn Zayd said: The meaning is: Jibril revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) what his Lord revealed to him. Sa'id said: He revealed to him ﴿Did He not find you an orphan﴾ [[Qur'an 93:6.]] up to His saying ﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾ [[Qur'an 94:4.]]. It was also said: He revealed to him that Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until he enters it, and forbidden to the nations until his community enters it.

Abu al-Hasan al-Thawri was asked about it and said: He revealed to him a secret, a secret from a secret, within a secret. Concerning this the poet says:

"Between the lovers is a secret that no speech reveals,
nor a pen that describes it to the creation.
A secret mixed with intimacy, facing it,
a light bewildered in a sea of perplexity."
[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 9/289.]]

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ [[Qur'an 53:11.]]. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far [al-Jahdari], and Qatadah recited "kadhdhaba" with a doubled dhal, meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not deny what it saw with his eye that night, but confirmed and verified it. The rest recited it with the light form, "kadhaba," meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not lie about what he saw, but confirmed it. The figurative meaning of the verse is: "The heart did not lie concerning what it saw," so the attribute is dropped, as in the poet's words:

"If you had been truthful in what you told me,
you would have escaped as Harith ibn Hisham escaped."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/93.]]

That is: "in that which you told me." Bandar ibn al-Hasan said: "Al-fu'ad" is the vessel of the heart; "the heart doubted concerning what it saw" means the origin, which is the heart.

They differed about who was seen. Some said: He saw Jibril, and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud. Others said: It is God, the Exalted. Then they differed about the meaning of the seeing. Some said: He placed his sight in his heart, so he saw Him in his heart and did not see Him with his eye. Others said: Rather, he saw Him with his eye.

Mention of those who said he saw Him with his eye:

Al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn informed me, saying: al-Fadl ibn al-Fadl told us, saying: Abu Ya'la Muhammad ibn Zuhayr al-Ablli told us, saying: Ibn Nuhwayh told us, saying: Salamah told us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq told us, saying: Ibn al-Taymi told us, from al-Mubarak ibn Fudalah, who said: al-Hasan used to swear by God, Mighty and Majestic, that Muhammad had seen his Lord.

'Aqil ibn Muhammad also informed me, saying: al-Mu'afa ibn Zakariyya told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jarir told us, saying: Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Mahran told us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from one who heard Ibn Abbas say: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾, he said: Muhammad saw his Lord.

With his chain from Ibn Humayd: Yahya ibn Wadih told us, saying: Isa ibn Ubayd told us, saying: I heard Ikrimah, and he was asked: Did Muhammad see his Lord? He said: Yes, he saw his Lord.

Also from Ibn Humayd: Hakkam told us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', concerning ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾: he said: He saw his Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Mention of those who said he did not see Him:

Abu Ubayd Allah al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Hafiz informed us, by my reading to him in my house, saying: Musa ibn Muhammad ibn Ali told us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Zuhayr told us, saying: Makki ibn Ibrahim told us, saying: Musa ibn Ubaydah told us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: One of the companions of the Messenger of God said: O Messenger of God, did you see your Lord? He said: "I saw Him twice, with my heart, and I did not see Him with my eye." [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 27/62; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 4/268, where the known wording is: "I did not see Him with my eye, and I saw Him with my heart twice."]] [120] Then he recited this verse: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾.

Similar was reported from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, from his father, and from Abu al-Aliyah, from Ibn Abbas.

Al-Hasan informed me, saying: Abu al-Qasim told us, from Ibn Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Hatim al-Tirmidhi, who said: My maternal grandfather Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Marzuq told us, saying: Affan ibn Muslim told us, saying: Hammam ibn Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq told us, who said: I said to Abu Dharr: If I had seen the Messenger of God (ﷺ), I would have asked him. He said: And what would you have asked him? I said: I would have asked him: Did he see his Lord, Mighty and Majestic? He said: I have indeed asked him, and he said: "I saw a light; how could I see Him?" [[Sharh Muslim by al-Nawawi: 3/12; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/93; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 3/5, with some variation in the wording of the hadith.]] [121]

Likewise, it is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about "The heart did not lie in what it saw," and he said: "I saw a light."
[[al-Musdar al-Sabiq, .]] [122], and Mujahid and Ikrimah narrated the like from Ibn 'Abbas.

There is a comprehensive hadith on this subject, which al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan informed me of, saying: Ibn Habash narrated to us, saying: 'Ali ibn Zanjawayh informed us, saying: Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn 'Uyaynah informed us, from Mujalid, from Sa'id, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith, who said: Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b met, and Ibn 'Abbas said: As for us, the Banu Hashim, we say that Muhammad saw his Lord twice. Ibn 'Abbas said: They love that intimate friendship (khullah) be for Ibrahim, speech for Musa, and vision for Muhammad. He said: Then Ka'b exclaimed "Allahu akbar" until the mountains echoed back to him, and then said:
"Indeed Allah, glory be to Him, divided His vision and His speech between Muhammad and Musa, peace be upon him. Musa spoke with Him, and Muhammad saw Him."
Mujalid said: al-Sha'bi said: Masruq informed me that he said to 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "O mother, did Muhammad (ﷺ) ever see his Lord, may He be exalted?" She said: "You have said a dreadful thing; my hair stood on end at it." I said: "Gently. Then I recited to her: ﴿Then he drew near and came down, and was two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾." She said: "Gently! Where are you going with this? He only saw Jibril in his true form. Whoever tells you that Muhammad saw his Lord has lied, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾. Whoever tells you that he knows the five matters of the Unseen has lied, and Allah, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour﴾, and the verse. Whoever tells you that Muhammad concealed any part of the revelation has lied, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿O Messenger, deliver what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾, and the verse."

'Abd al-Razzaq said: I mentioned this hadith to 'Umar, and he said: "'Aishah is not more knowledgeable than Ibn 'Abbas in our view."

﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ That is: over what he saw.

'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Aishah, Masruq, al-Nakha'i, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Ya'qub read ﴿Afatamrunahu﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and without an alif, meaning "Will you then deny him," and Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading, saying:
"Because they did not dispute with him; rather, they denied him. The Arabs say: 'Maraytu al-rajul haqqahu' when you denied the man his right." The poet said:
"If you have forsaken a brother of truthfulness and honor, you have indeed denied a brother who never denied you."
That is, you denied him.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Talhah ibn Musarrif read ﴿Afatumrunahu﴾ with a damma on the ta' and without an alif, meaning "Will you cause him doubt and make him suspicious." The rest read ﴿Afatumarunahu﴾ with the alif and a damma on the ta', meaning "Will you then argue with him," and this is the choice of Abu Hatim.

And in a hadith: "Do not dispute about the Qur'an, for disputing over it is disbelief."
[123] [[Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/619, no. 2860.]]

And He certainly saw him another time, a second descent (nazlah ukhra), and He called it a "descent" by way of metaphor. This is because Jibril (Gabriel) was seen by the Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ) in the form in which he was created, twice: once at the highest horizon on earth, and once near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha) in the heavens. This is the view of ʿĀ'ishah and most of the scholars, and it is the preferred one, because He linked the seeing with a place when He said ʿinda sidrat al-muntahā, and because He said nazlatan ukhrā, whose implied meaning is: "He saw him descending another time." Attributing place and descent, which is movement, to God is impossible. Also, He said nazlatan ukhrā, and it is not reported in any hadith that the Prophet ﷺ saw his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, before the night of the Ascension (mi'raj) and then saw Him again that night. What supports this is:

ʿaqil ibn Muhammad informed me that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Muhammad ibn Jarir, from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, who said: ʿAbd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi narrated to us, who said: Dawud ibn ʿAmir narrated to us, from Masruq, that ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has greatly slandered Allah."

He said: I was reclining, so I sat up and said: "O Mother of the Believers, grant me a moment and do not hurry. Tell me about the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And he certainly saw him another time﴾ and ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾." She said: "It was only Jibril. He saw him in his form in which he was created, twice: once when he descended from the sky to the earth, filling the greatest span between the sky and the earth, and once near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary." She said: "And I was the first to ask the Prophet about this verse, and he said: 'It is Jibril.'" [124]

ʿinda sidrat al-muntahā: ʿinda is connected to his saying ra'āhu (he saw him). The sidrah is the lote-tree (shajrat al-nabiq). It was called "the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary" because the knowledge of every knower ends at it.

Hilal ibn Sayyaf said: Ibn ʿAbbas asked Kaʿb about the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary while I was present, and Kaʿb said: "It is a lote-tree at the base of the Throne, on the heads of the bearers of the Throne, and the knowledge of creation ends at it, and what lies beyond it is unseen, which none knows except Allah, the Glorified."

Ibn Masʿud said: it was named so because what descends from above it and what ascends from below it, of the command of Allah, the Exalted, ends at it. When one who ascends to it from the earth reaches it, it is seized from it. It was also said: it is because the spirits of believers ascend and end at it. And it was said: it is because everyone who dies upon the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah and his way ends at it.

Al-Rabiʿ narrated from Abu al-ʿĀliyah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: When the Prophet ﷺ was taken on the Night Journey (usriya bihi), he reached the Lote-tree, and it was said to him: "This is the Lote-tree, to which every one of your community who follows your Sunnah will come." Behold, from its root flow rivers of water unaltered (ghayru asin) up to His saying: "purified" (muṣaffā). It is a tree under whose shade a rider travels for seventy years without crossing it, and one of its leaves covers the whole community.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Shaybah narrated to us, who said: al-Tanukhi narrated to us, who said: ʿUbayd ibn Yaʿish narrated to us, who said: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, from Yahya ibn ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, from his grandmother Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ mention the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and he said:

"A rider travels in the shade of its branch for a hundred years, and a hundred riders can take shelter in its branches. In it are golden butterflies, and its fruits are like jars (qilal)." [125] [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 4/86, with slight variation]]

Muqatil said: It is a tree such that if one of its leaves were placed on the earth, it would light up for the people of the earth; it bears ornaments, garments and fruits of every colour. And if a man were to ride a swift she-camel and go around its trunk, he would not reach the place from which he set out until old age killed him. It is the Tuba (ṭūbā) which Allah mentioned in Surat al-Raʿd. I have fully described its attributes in the account of the Night Journey.

ʿindahā jannat al-maʾwā, idh yaghshā al-sidrata mā yaghshā (Near it is the Garden of Refuge, when there covers the Lote-tree what covers).

Ibn Masʿud and his companions said: "Golden butterflies." This is also the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and he traced it back to the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Hasan said: The light of the Lord of Majesty covered it and it became radiant. It was also said: the angels.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I saw on every leaf of it an angel standing, glorifying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." [126]

Al-Rabiʿ narrated from Abu Hurayrah or another, who said: When the Prophet ﷺ was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree. He said: The light of creation covered it, and the angels covered it out of love for Allah, like crows when they alight on a tree.

He said: Then He spoke to him at that moment and said: "Ask."

In a hadith: the Prophet ﷺ said: "Then there covered it [in the source: yaghshāhā] a fluttering of green birds." [127] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/97.]]

Al-Suddi said: "Of birds, above it."

Anas narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "I reached the Lote-tree, and I knew that it was the Lote-tree; I know its leaves and its fruit, and when its ripe fruit is like jars, and its leaves like elephants' ears. When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered it, it turned into rubies and emeralds, until no one can describe it. Near it is the Garden of Refuge." [128] [[See Jami al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 27/72071; the hadith is not one single report.]]

Ibn ʿAbbas said: It is the right side of the Throne, and it is the station of the martyrs, like His saying: ﴿For them are the Gardens of Refuge﴾.

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad informed us, saying: Abu ʿAbd Allah ʿUmar ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Harith al-Qadibani narrated to us. He said: ʿAli ibn al-ʿAbbas al-Muqanaʿi narrated to us, who said: Maymun ibn al-Asbaʿ narrated to us, who said: Yahya ibn Salih al-Wuhadhi narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Sulayman ibn Hamzah al-Basri narrated to us, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Qays narrated to us, who said: I heard ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr recite this verse as ʿindahā jannah (with a hā' at the end), meaning "the garden of spending the night" (jannat al-mabit).

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Talhah ibn Muhammad and ʿUbayd Allah ibn Ahmad narrated to us, both saying: Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid narrated to us, who said: Abu Sadaqah narrated to me, who said: Abu al-Asbat narrated to us, who said: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, from ʿAli ibn al-Qasim al-Kindi, from Musa ibn ʿUbaydah, who said: I heard Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi recite jannah al-maʾwā (with a hā'). Mujahid said: he means ajannahu (He covered him), and the hā' in this reading refers to the Prophet ﷺ.

Abu Hatim said: This is the reading of ʿAli and Anas, meaning "covered him." Al-Akhfash said: "reached him" (adrakahu).

Mā zāgha al-baṣaru wa-mā ṭagha (His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress): that is, he did not go beyond what he was commanded, nor did he turn away from what he was sent to see.

Laqad raʾā min āyāti rabbihi al-kubrā (He certainly saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord): that is, the greatest sign.

Ibn Masʿud said: He saw a green fluttering from Paradise that filled the horizon. Al-Dahhak said: the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yazid and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: He saw Jibril in his form which he has in the heavens. It was also said: the Ascension (al-miʿraj), and what was shown to him that night in his journey and his return and his beginning. The proof is His saying: ﴿So that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ ...

Afa-ra'aytumu al-lāt (Have you considered al-Lat?). The common reading is with the tā' lightened. It is derived from (Allah), and a tā' was added to it, so it became feminine. Just as it is said ʿumar for the male, then ʿumrah for the female, and ʿabbās and ʿabbāsah. Likewise the polytheists named their idols after the names of Allah: they said from Allah (al-Lāt), and from al-ʿAzīz (al-ʿUzzā).

Qatadah said: As for al-Lat, it was at al-Ta'if. Ibn Zayd said: al-Lat was a house at Nakhlah which Quraysh worshipped.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Abu Salih read al-Lāt with the tā' doubled, and they said: he was a man who used to pound (yaltu) sawiq for the pilgrims. When he died, they devoted themselves to his grave and worshipped him. Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Salih that he was at al-Ta'if, and he used to attend to their gods and pound sawiq for them; when he died, they worshipped him.

Mujahid said: He was a man on the top of a mountain who had goats from which he would collect butter and take aqit (dried curd), and gather their milk, and then prepare from it hays (a mixture of dates, aqit and ghee) which he fed to the pilgrims. He was at Batn Nakhlah, and when he died they worshipped him, and he is al-Lat. Al-Kalbi said: He was a man from Thaqif called Sakhrah ibn Ghanm, who used to melt butter and place it on a rock, and the Arabs would come and smear their swords with it. When the man died, Thaqif took the rock to their dwellings and worshipped it; the idol of al-Ta'if was based on the placing of al-Lat.

Wal-ʿUzzā: they differed about it. Mujahid said: It is a tree belonging to Ghatafan, which they worshipped.

It was this that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Khalid ibn al-Walid against, and he cut it down, and Khalid began striking it with an axe, saying:

"O ʿUzza, disbelief in you! No glory to you! Indeed I have seen that Allah has humiliated you."

From it there came out a female devil, with hair flowing and crying out woe, placing her hand on her head. It is said that Khalid returned to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "I have cut it down." He said: "What did you see?" He said: "I saw nothing." He said: "You have not cut it." So he went back to it with the axe, uprooted it and pulled out its root, and out came a naked woman, and he killed her. Then he returned to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of that, and he said: "That was al-ʿUzza, and she will never be worshipped again." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/100.]] [129]

Al-Dahhak said: It was an idol of Ghatafan, which Saʿd ibn Zalim al-Ghatafani set up for them. He came to Mecca and saw al-Safa and al-Marwah, and saw the people of Mecca going around between them. He returned to [Batn Nakhlah] and said to his people:

"The people of Mecca have al-Safa and al-Marwah and you do not have them, and they have a god they worship and you do not have one." They said: "What do you command us?" He said: "I will make for you the same." He took a stone from al-Safa and a stone from al-Marwah, and carried them to Batn Nakhlah. He placed the one from al-Safa and said: "This is al-Safa," then he placed the one he had taken from al-Marwah and said: "This is al-Marwah." Then he took three stones and leaned them against a tree and said: "This is your lord." They began to go around between the two stones and worship the stones, until the Messenger of Allah conquered Mecca, and he ordered the stones removed, and sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to al-ʿUzza, and he cut them down.

Ibn Zayd said: It was a house at al-Ta'if which Thaqif worshipped.

Wa-manāt: Ibn Kathir read it with a long vowel (al-madd), and similarly al-Shammuni narrated from Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, and recited:

"Has there not reached the Taym ibn ʿAbd Manat, against the Shanʾ, between us, Ibn Tamim?"

The rest read it short.

Qatadah said: It is stones that were worshipped. Ibn Zayd said: a house at al-Mushallal worshipped by the Banu Kaʿb.

Al-Dahhak said: Manat was an idol of Hudhayl and Khuza'ah, worshipped by the people of Mecca. It was also said that its etymology is from nā' al-najm yanūʾ nawʾan (the rising of the star). Some said: al-Lat, al-ʿUzza and Manat are idols of stone which were inside the Ka'bah, and they worshipped them.

The readers differed over stopping on al-Lat and Manat: some stopped on them with a hā', and some with a tā'. Some said: Everything in the Qur'an written with a tā' is stopped on with a tā', such as bi-niʿmati rabbika and shajarat al-zaqqum and the like; and whatever is written with a hā', stopping on it is with a hā'. Others said: The preference in every word that is not in construct (idafah) is to be with a hā', like raḥmatun min rabbī and shajaratan takhruju; and whatever is in construct is permissible with a hā' or a tā': the tā' for the construct and the hā' because it is standing alone without the tā'.

As for His saying, the Third, the Other (al-thālithata al-ukhrā): the Arabs do not say "the third, other" (al-thālithah ukhrā); rather "ukhrā" is an adjective of the second. The scholars differed about its explanation. Al-Khalil said: He only said that to match the endings of the verses, like His saying: ﴿needs (maʾārib) other﴾, and He did not say "akhar." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: There is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse; its meaning is: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-ʿUzza the other, and Manat the third?" The meaning of the verse: "Have you considered, O you who claim that al-Lat, al-ʿUzza and Manat are daughters of Allah,"

﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him? That is then an unjust division.﴾ Ibn Kathir's transmitters al-Qawwas and al-Bazzi read it with hamzah (ḍi'zā); the rest without hamzah. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: that is, an unjust division, since you assigned to your Lord what you dislike for yourselves. Mujahid and Muqatil: crooked. Al-Hasan: not balanced. Ibn Sirin: not equal, that they should have males and Allah should have females. Al-Dahhak: deficient. Sufyan: diminished. Ibn Zayd: contrary.

Al-Kisa'i said: It is said: ḍāza yaḍīzu ḍayzan; ḍāza yaḍūzu ḍawzan; ḍāza yuḍāzu ḍa'zan, meaning he wronged and diminished. A poet said:

"The Banu Asad were wronged in their judgment, when they made the head like the tail."

Al-Akhfash recited:

"If you withdraw from us, we shall diminish you; and if you are absent, your arrow is unfit and your nose is humbled."

The form ḍīzā in terms of grammar is fu'lā with the fa' pronounced with a ḍammah, because it is an adjective, and adjectives are only fu'lā with a ḍammah, such as ḥublā, unthā and yusrā; or fa'lā with a fatḥah, such as ghaḍbā, sakrā and ʿaṭshā. There is no fu'lā with a kasrah in the fa' among adjectives in Arabic; it occurs only in nouns, such as difrā, dhikrā and shi'rā. The historian said: They disliked the ḍammah on the ḍād and feared the ya' turning into waw, and it comes from the ya' roots, so they gave the ḍād a kasrah for this reason, as they said for the plural of abyad: bīḍ, the original being buwḍ, like ḥumr and ṣafr. As for the one who said ḍāza yaḍūzu, its noun is ḍawzā, like shawrā.

Inna hiya, meaning these idols, illā asmā'un sammaytumūhā antum wa-ābā'ukum mā anzala Allāhu bihā min sulṭān (They are only names which you and your fathers have named; Allah has sent down no authority for them). The common reading is with yā' (in yattabiʿūna); ʿIsa read it with tā'. Illā al-ẓanna (except conjecture) in their saying that they are gods and that they are their intercessors, wa-mā tahwā al-anfusu (and what the souls desire). And He has certainly sent them guidance from their Lord, to show that they are not gods, and that worship is fit only for Allah, the One, the Subduer.

And He certainly saw him another time, a second descent (nazlah ukhra), and He called it a "descent" by way of metaphor. This is because Jibril (Gabriel) was seen by the Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ) in the form in which he was created, twice: once at the highest horizon on earth, and once near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha) in the heavens. This is the view of ʿĀ'ishah and most of the scholars, and it is the preferred one, because He linked the seeing with a place when He said ʿinda sidrat al-muntahā, and because He said nazlatan ukhrā, whose implied meaning is: "He saw him descending another time." Attributing place and descent, which is movement, to God is impossible. Also, He said nazlatan ukhrā, and it is not reported in any hadith that the Prophet ﷺ saw his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, before the night of the Ascension (mi'raj) and then saw Him again that night. What supports this is:

ʿaqil ibn Muhammad informed me that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Muhammad ibn Jarir, from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, who said: ʿAbd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi narrated to us, who said: Dawud ibn ʿAmir narrated to us, from Masruq, that ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has greatly slandered Allah."

He said: I was reclining, so I sat up and said: "O Mother of the Believers, grant me a moment and do not hurry. Tell me about the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And he certainly saw him another time﴾ and ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾." She said: "It was only Jibril. He saw him in his form in which he was created, twice: once when he descended from the sky to the earth, filling the greatest span between the sky and the earth, and once near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary." She said: "And I was the first to ask the Prophet about this verse, and he said: 'It is Jibril.'" [124]

ʿinda sidrat al-muntahā: ʿinda is connected to his saying ra'āhu (he saw him). The sidrah is the lote-tree (shajrat al-nabiq). It was called "the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary" because the knowledge of every knower ends at it.

Hilal ibn Sayyaf said: Ibn ʿAbbas asked Kaʿb about the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary while I was present, and Kaʿb said: "It is a lote-tree at the base of the Throne, on the heads of the bearers of the Throne, and the knowledge of creation ends at it, and what lies beyond it is unseen, which none knows except Allah, the Glorified."

Ibn Masʿud said: it was named so because what descends from above it and what ascends from below it, of the command of Allah, the Exalted, ends at it. When one who ascends to it from the earth reaches it, it is seized from it. It was also said: it is because the spirits of believers ascend and end at it. And it was said: it is because everyone who dies upon the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah and his way ends at it.

Al-Rabiʿ narrated from Abu al-ʿĀliyah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: When the Prophet ﷺ was taken on the Night Journey (usriya bihi), he reached the Lote-tree, and it was said to him: "This is the Lote-tree, to which every one of your community who follows your Sunnah will come." Behold, from its root flow rivers of water unaltered (ghayru asin) up to His saying: "purified" (muṣaffā). It is a tree under whose shade a rider travels for seventy years without crossing it, and one of its leaves covers the whole community.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Shaybah narrated to us, who said: al-Tanukhi narrated to us, who said: ʿUbayd ibn Yaʿish narrated to us, who said: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, from Yahya ibn ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, from his grandmother Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ mention the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and he said:

"A rider travels in the shade of its branch for a hundred years, and a hundred riders can take shelter in its branches. In it are golden butterflies, and its fruits are like jars (qilal)." [125] [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 4/86, with slight variation]]

Muqatil said: It is a tree such that if one of its leaves were placed on the earth, it would light up for the people of the earth; it bears ornaments, garments and fruits of every colour. And if a man were to ride a swift she-camel and go around its trunk, he would not reach the place from which he set out until old age killed him. It is the Tuba (ṭūbā) which Allah mentioned in Surat al-Raʿd. I have fully described its attributes in the account of the Night Journey.

ʿindahā jannat al-maʾwā, idh yaghshā al-sidrata mā yaghshā (Near it is the Garden of Refuge, when there covers the Lote-tree what covers).

Ibn Masʿud and his companions said: "Golden butterflies." This is also the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and he traced it back to the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Hasan said: The light of the Lord of Majesty covered it and it became radiant. It was also said: the angels.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I saw on every leaf of it an angel standing, glorifying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." [126]

Al-Rabiʿ narrated from Abu Hurayrah or another, who said: When the Prophet ﷺ was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree. He said: The light of creation covered it, and the angels covered it out of love for Allah, like crows when they alight on a tree.

He said: Then He spoke to him at that moment and said: "Ask."

In a hadith: the Prophet ﷺ said: "Then there covered it [in the source: yaghshāhā] a fluttering of green birds." [127] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/97.]]

Al-Suddi said: "Of birds, above it."

Anas narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "I reached the Lote-tree, and I knew that it was the Lote-tree; I know its leaves and its fruit, and when its ripe fruit is like jars, and its leaves like elephants' ears. When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered it, it turned into rubies and emeralds, until no one can describe it. Near it is the Garden of Refuge." [128] [[See Jami al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 27/72071; the hadith is not one single report.]]

Ibn ʿAbbas said: It is the right side of the Throne, and it is the station of the martyrs, like His saying: ﴿For them are the Gardens of Refuge﴾.

Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad informed us, saying: Abu ʿAbd Allah ʿUmar ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Harith al-Qadibani narrated to us. He said: ʿAli ibn al-ʿAbbas al-Muqanaʿi narrated to us, who said: Maymun ibn al-Asbaʿ narrated to us, who said: Yahya ibn Salih al-Wuhadhi narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Sulayman ibn Hamzah al-Basri narrated to us, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Qays narrated to us, who said: I heard ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr recite this verse as ʿindahā jannah (with a hā' at the end), meaning "the garden of spending the night" (jannat al-mabit).

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Talhah ibn Muhammad and ʿUbayd Allah ibn Ahmad narrated to us, both saying: Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid narrated to us, who said: Abu Sadaqah narrated to me, who said: Abu al-Asbat narrated to us, who said: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, from ʿAli ibn al-Qasim al-Kindi, from Musa ibn ʿUbaydah, who said: I heard Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi recite jannah al-maʾwā (with a hā'). Mujahid said: he means ajannahu (He covered him), and the hā' in this reading refers to the Prophet ﷺ.

Abu Hatim said: This is the reading of ʿAli and Anas, meaning "covered him." Al-Akhfash said: "reached him" (adrakahu).

Mā zāgha al-baṣaru wa-mā ṭagha (His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress): that is, he did not go beyond what he was commanded, nor did he turn away from what he was sent to see.

Laqad raʾā min āyāti rabbihi al-kubrā (He certainly saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord): that is, the greatest sign.

Ibn Masʿud said: He saw a green fluttering from Paradise that filled the horizon. Al-Dahhak said: the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yazid and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: He saw Jibril in his form which he has in the heavens. It was also said: the Ascension (al-miʿraj), and what was shown to him that night in his journey and his return and his beginning. The proof is His saying: ﴿So that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ ...

Afa-ra'aytumu al-lāt (Have you considered al-Lat?). The common reading is with the tā' lightened. It is derived from (Allah), and a tā' was added to it, so it became feminine. Just as it is said ʿumar for the male, then ʿumrah for the female, and ʿabbās and ʿabbāsah. Likewise the polytheists named their idols after the names of Allah: they said from Allah (al-Lāt), and from al-ʿAzīz (al-ʿUzzā).

Qatadah said: As for al-Lat, it was at al-Ta'if. Ibn Zayd said: al-Lat was a house at Nakhlah which Quraysh worshipped.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Abu Salih read al-Lāt with the tā' doubled, and they said: he was a man who used to pound (yaltu) sawiq for the pilgrims. When he died, they devoted themselves to his grave and worshipped him. Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Salih that he was at al-Ta'if, and he used to attend to their gods and pound sawiq for them; when he died, they worshipped him.

Mujahid said: He was a man on the top of a mountain who had goats from which he would collect butter and take aqit (dried curd), and gather their milk, and then prepare from it hays (a mixture of dates, aqit and ghee) which he fed to the pilgrims. He was at Batn Nakhlah, and when he died they worshipped him, and he is al-Lat. Al-Kalbi said: He was a man from Thaqif called Sakhrah ibn Ghanm, who used to melt butter and place it on a rock, and the Arabs would come and smear their swords with it. When the man died, Thaqif took the rock to their dwellings and worshipped it; the idol of al-Ta'if was based on the placing of al-Lat.

Wal-ʿUzzā: they differed about it. Mujahid said: It is a tree belonging to Ghatafan, which they worshipped.

It was this that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Khalid ibn al-Walid against, and he cut it down, and Khalid began striking it with an axe, saying:

"O ʿUzza, disbelief in you! No glory to you! Indeed I have seen that Allah has humiliated you."

From it there came out a female devil, with hair flowing and crying out woe, placing her hand on her head. It is said that Khalid returned to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "I have cut it down." He said: "What did you see?" He said: "I saw nothing." He said: "You have not cut it." So he went back to it with the axe, uprooted it and pulled out its root, and out came a naked woman, and he killed her. Then he returned to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of that, and he said: "That was al-ʿUzza, and she will never be worshipped again." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/100.]] [129]

Al-Dahhak said: It was an idol of Ghatafan, which Saʿd ibn Zalim al-Ghatafani set up for them. He came to Mecca and saw al-Safa and al-Marwah, and saw the people of Mecca going around between them. He returned to [Batn Nakhlah] and said to his people:

"The people of Mecca have al-Safa and al-Marwah and you do not have them, and they have a god they worship and you do not have one." They said: "What do you command us?" He said: "I will make for you the same." He took a stone from al-Safa and a stone from al-Marwah, and carried them to Batn Nakhlah. He placed the one from al-Safa and said: "This is al-Safa," then he placed the one he had taken from al-Marwah and said: "This is al-Marwah." Then he took three stones and leaned them against a tree and said: "This is your lord." They began to go around between the two stones and worship the stones, until the Messenger of Allah conquered Mecca, and he ordered the stones removed, and sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to al-ʿUzza, and he cut them down.

Ibn Zayd said: It was a house at al-Ta'if which Thaqif worshipped.

Wa-manāt: Ibn Kathir read it with a long vowel (al-madd), and similarly al-Shammuni narrated from Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, and recited:

"Has there not reached the Taym ibn ʿAbd Manat, against the Shanʾ, between us, Ibn Tamim?"

The rest read it short.

Qatadah said: It is stones that were worshipped. Ibn Zayd said: a house at al-Mushallal worshipped by the Banu Kaʿb.

Al-Dahhak said: Manat was an idol of Hudhayl and Khuza'ah, worshipped by the people of Mecca. It was also said that its etymology is from nā' al-najm yanūʾ nawʾan (the rising of the star). Some said: al-Lat, al-ʿUzza and Manat are idols of stone which were inside the Ka'bah, and they worshipped them.

The readers differed over stopping on al-Lat and Manat: some stopped on them with a hā', and some with a tā'. Some said: Everything in the Qur'an written with a tā' is stopped on with a tā', such as bi-niʿmati rabbika and shajarat al-zaqqum and the like; and whatever is written with a hā', stopping on it is with a hā'. Others said: The preference in every word that is not in construct (idafah) is to be with a hā', like raḥmatun min rabbī and shajaratan takhruju; and whatever is in construct is permissible with a hā' or a tā': the tā' for the construct and the hā' because it is standing alone without the tā'.

As for His saying, the Third, the Other (al-thālithata al-ukhrā): the Arabs do not say "the third, other" (al-thālithah ukhrā); rather "ukhrā" is an adjective of the second. The scholars differed about its explanation. Al-Khalil said: He only said that to match the endings of the verses, like His saying: ﴿needs (maʾārib) other﴾, and He did not say "akhar." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: There is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse; its meaning is: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-ʿUzza the other, and Manat the third?" The meaning of the verse: "Have you considered, O you who claim that al-Lat, al-ʿUzza and Manat are daughters of Allah,"

﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him? That is then an unjust division.﴾ Ibn Kathir's transmitters al-Qawwas and al-Bazzi read it with hamzah (ḍi'zā); the rest without hamzah. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: that is, an unjust division, since you assigned to your Lord what you dislike for yourselves. Mujahid and Muqatil: crooked. Al-Hasan: not balanced. Ibn Sirin: not equal, that they should have males and Allah should have females. Al-Dahhak: deficient. Sufyan: diminished. Ibn Zayd: contrary.

Al-Kisa'i said: It is said: ḍāza yaḍīzu ḍayzan; ḍāza yaḍūzu ḍawzan; ḍāza yuḍāzu ḍa'zan, meaning he wronged and diminished. A poet said:

"The Banu Asad were wronged in their judgment, when they made the head like the tail."

Al-Akhfash recited:

"If you withdraw from us, we shall diminish you; and if you are absent, your arrow is unfit and your nose is humbled."

The form ḍīzā in terms of grammar is fu'lā with the fa' pronounced with a ḍammah, because it is an adjective, and adjectives are only fu'lā with a ḍammah, such as ḥublā, unthā and yusrā; or fa'lā with a fatḥah, such as ghaḍbā, sakrā and ʿaṭshā. There is no fu'lā with a kasrah in the fa' among adjectives in Arabic; it occurs only in nouns, such as difrā, dhikrā and shi'rā. The historian said: They disliked the ḍammah on the ḍād and feared the ya' turning into waw, and it comes from the ya' roots, so they gave the ḍād a kasrah for this reason, as they said for the plural of abyad: bīḍ, the original being buwḍ, like ḥumr and ṣafr. As for the one who said ḍāza yaḍūzu, its noun is ḍawzā, like shawrā.

Inna hiya, meaning these idols, illā asmā'un sammaytumūhā antum wa-ābā'ukum mā anzala Allāhu bihā min sulṭān (They are only names which you and your fathers have named; Allah has sent down no authority for them). The common reading is with yā' (in yattabiʿūna); ʿIsa read it with tā'. Illā al-ẓanna (except conjecture) in their saying that they are gods and that they are their intercessors, wa-mā tahwā al-anfusu (and what the souls desire). And He has certainly sent them guidance from their Lord, to show that they are not gods, and that worship is fit only for Allah, the One, the Subduer.

And He certainly saw him another time, a second descent (nazlah ukhra), and He called it a "descent" by way of metaphor. This is because Jibril (Gabriel) was seen by the Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ) in the form in which he was created, twice: once at the highest horizon on earth, and once near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha) in the heavens. This is the view of ʿĀ'ishah and most of the scholars, and it is the preferred one, because He linked the seeing with a place when He said ʿinda sidrat al-muntahā, and because He said nazlatan ukhrā, whose implied meaning is: "He saw him descending another time." Attributing place and descent, which is movement, to God is impossible. Also, He said nazlatan ukhrā, and it is not reported in any hadith that the Prophet ﷺ saw his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, before the night of the Ascension (mi'raj) and then saw Him again that night. What supports this is:

ʿaqil ibn Muhammad informed me that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Muhammad ibn Jarir, from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, who said: ʿAbd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi narrated to us, who said: Dawud ibn ʿAmir narrated to us, from Masruq, that ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has greatly slandered Allah."

He said: I was reclining, so I sat up and said: "O Mother of the Believers, grant me a moment and do not hurry. Tell me about the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And he certainly saw him another time﴾ and ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾." She said: "It was only Jibril. He saw him in his form in which he was created, twice: once when he descended from the sky to the earth, filling the greatest span between the sky and the earth, and once near the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary." She said: "And I was the first to ask the Prophet about this verse, and he said: 'It is Jibril.'" [124]

ʿinda sidrat al-muntahā: ʿinda is connected to his saying ra'āhu (he saw him). The sidrah is the lote-tree (shajrat al-nabiq). It was called "the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary" because the knowledge of every knower ends at it.

Hilal ibn Sayyaf said: Ibn ʿAbbas asked Kaʿb about the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary while I was present, and Kaʿb said: "It is a lote-tree at the base of the Throne, on the heads of the bearers of the Throne, and the knowledge of creation ends at it, and what lies beyond it is unseen, which none knows except Allah, the Glorified."

Ibn Masʿud said: it was named so because what descends from above it and what ascends from below it, of the command of Allah, the Exalted, ends at it. When one who ascends to it from the earth reaches it, it is seized from it. It was also said: it is because the spirits of believers ascend and end at it. And it was said: it is because everyone who dies upon the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah and his way ends at it.

Al-Rabiʿ narrated from Abu al-ʿĀliyah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: When the Prophet ﷺ was taken on the Night Journey (usriya bihi), he reached the Lote-tree, and it was said to him: "This is the Lote-tree, to which every one of your community who follows your Sunnah will come." Behold, from its root flow rivers of water unaltered (ghayru asin) up to His saying: "purified" (muṣaffā). It is a tree under whose shade a rider travels for seventy years without crossing it, and one of its leaves covers the whole community.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Shaybah narrated to us, who said: al-Tanukhi narrated to us, who said: ʿUbayd ibn Yaʿish narrated to us, who said: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, from Yahya ibn ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, from his grandmother Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ mention the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and he said:

"A rider travels in the shade of its branch for a hundred years, and a hundred riders can take shelter in its branches. In it are golden butterflies, and its fruits are like jars (qilal)." [125] [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 4/86, with slight variation]]

Muqatil said: It is a tree such that if one of its leaves were placed on the earth, it would light up for the people of the earth; it bears ornaments, garments and fruits of every colour. And if a man were to ride a swift she-camel and go around its trunk, he would not reach the place from which he set out until old age killed him. It is the Tuba (ṭūbā) which Allah mentioned in Surat al-Raʿd. I have fully described its attributes in the account of the Night Journey.

ʿindahā jannat al-maʾwā, idh yaghshā al-sidrata mā yaghshā (Near it is the Garden of Refuge, when there covers the Lote-tree what covers).

Ibn Masʿud and his companions said: "Golden butterflies." This is also the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and he traced it back to the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Hasan said: The light of the Lord of Majesty covered it and it became radiant. It was also said: the angels.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I saw on every leaf of it an angel standing, glorifying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." [126]

Al-Rabiʿ narrated from Abu Hurayrah or another, who said: When the Prophet ﷺ was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree. He said: The light of creation covered it, and the angels covered it out of love for Allah, like crows when they alight on a tree.

He said: Then He spoke to him at that moment and said: "Ask."

In a hadith: the Prophet ﷺ said: "Then there covered it [in the source: yaghshāhā] a fluttering of green birds." [127] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 17/97.]]

Al-Suddi said: "Of birds, above it."

Anas narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "I reached the Lote-tree, and I knew that it was the Lote-tree; I know its leaves and its fruit, and when its ripe fruit is like jars, and its leaves like elephants' ears. When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered it, it turned into rubies and emeralds, until no one can describe it. Near it is the Garden of Refuge."
